opus-5.5.text:
Health care is a really interesting setting because it makes the abstract questions concrete. In a lot of general-purpose evaluation, we talk about harm in fairly generic terms: toxicity, bias, misinformation. Those matter, but in a clinical context the consequences are much more specific and often much more severe. A wrong answer isn't just embarrassing; it can mean a missed diagnosis, a bad dosage, or a patient deciding not to seek care.

So one shift is that you have to think about harm relative to an actual workflow. Who is using the model? A clinician who can catch errors, or a patient who may take the output at face value? Is it drafting a note, summarizing a chart, or answering a medical question directly? The same model output can be harmless in one setting and dangerous in another, so evaluation has to be tied to deployment context rather than treated as a property of the model in isolation.

A second shift is around measurement validity. Many existing benchmarks are multiple-choice exam-style questions, and doing well on a licensing-exam-type test tells you something, but it's not the same as being safe in practice. Real clinical interactions are messy, underspecified, and longitudinal. So part of the work is building evaluations that reflect that, and being honest about what a given benchmark can and can't tell you.

Third, health care forces you to take subgroup performance seriously. Averages hide a lot. If a model works well on average but systematically worse for certain populations, because of how they describe symptoms, language differences, or gaps in the training data, that's a real equity harm, and it often reinforces disparities that already exist in medicine.

And finally, there's the question of who defines harm. In health care you have clinicians, patients, regulators, and institutions, and they don't always agree. Good evaluation needs input from those stakeholders, not just from ML researchers choosing metrics that are convenient to compute. In that sense, health care is a good forcing function: it pushes us toward evaluation that is more contextual and more rigorous, and I think those lessons carry back to how we should evaluate these systems more broadly.

r001.rationale: It contrasts generic harms in general-purpose evaluation with concrete, specific clinical consequences such as missed diagnoses and bad dosages.

r002.rationale: It discusses medical workflows and users, but does not identify the assumption that models will not be used for medical decision-making as a source of evaluation blind spots.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think health care is actually a really useful lens, because it forces you to be concrete about what harm means. In a lot of general-purpose evaluation, we talk about harm in a fairly abstract way, like toxicity scores or refusal rates, and those are proxies. In health care you can't get away with the proxy. The question becomes, did this output lead to a worse clinical decision, did it delay care, did it give someone false reassurance about a symptom they should have taken seriously. Those are outcomes you can actually define and, in principle, measure.

The second thing it changes is that harm is distributional. Medicine already has a long history of knowing that the same intervention does not perform the same across populations, and the same is true of a model. A model can look great on aggregate benchmarks and still be systematically worse for certain patient groups, certain languages, certain presentations of disease. So in health care we tend to ask, who is this failing, not just how often does it fail. That's a mindset I think the broader evaluation community could borrow.

And the third piece is that health care gives you a notion of the standard of care. There's an existing baseline, which is what a competent clinician would do, and that lets you ask whether the model is better or worse than the status quo, rather than better or worse than some idealized perfect answer. That matters, because the counterfactual in many settings is not a doctor, it's no information at all, or a search engine. So the harm calculus is different depending on who is actually using the system and what they would have done otherwise.

What makes it hard is that the stakes mean you can't just run the model loose and observe the harms. You need to simulate, you need expert review, and you have to be honest that those evaluations are themselves imperfect. But I'd rather be in a domain where the harm is at least well-defined and people argue about measurement, than in one where we're still arguing about what harm even means.

r001.rationale: The response says health care forces evaluators to be concrete about harm and describes clinical outcomes that can be defined and measured, contrasting this with abstract general-purpose proxies.

r002.rationale: The response discusses clinical decisions and evaluation gaps, but does not identify an assumption that language models will not be used for medical decision-making as a source of blind spots.

astra-6.text:
I think health care makes the question of harm much more concrete. You have to ask: Who is using the model, what decision are they making, and what happens if the model gets it wrong? A model helping a clinician draft a note is very different from a model giving a patient advice about whether to seek treatment. Even if they produce the same incorrect statement, the consequences can be quite different.

That also changes what you measure. Average accuracy is useful, but it doesn’t tell you whether the errors are clinically consequential, or whether they fall disproportionately on a particular group of patients. You might care much more about missing an urgent condition than about some other kind of mistake.

And you have to evaluate the interaction with the person using the system. Does a clinician catch the error, or does a fluent answer make them more likely to accept it? So the unit of evaluation becomes the model in a particular workflow, with particular users and patients. Testing the model in isolation only gets you part of the way there.

r001.rationale: The response says health care makes harm “much more concrete” by tying it to who uses the model, the decision, and the consequences of errors.

r002.rationale: The response calls for evaluating models in specific medical workflows, but does not identify the assumption that models will not be used for medical decision-making as a blind spot in general-purpose evaluations.

sol-6.1.text:
Health care gives you a more concrete way to think about harm, because there’s a decision being made and there are consequences for a patient. So rather than asking only whether a model generates something offensive or factually incorrect, you can ask: Could this response lead to an inappropriate treatment? Could it delay someone seeking care? And who is most likely to be affected?

The context matters a lot. A model helping a clinician draft a note has a different risk profile from a model giving medical advice directly to a patient. Even the same error can have very different consequences depending on who sees it and what safeguards are around it.

So I think health care pushes us to evaluate the whole system: the model, the person using it, and the decision that follows. Accuracy is part of that, but you also want to understand uncertainty, whether people rely on the output appropriately, and whether the benefits and harms are distributed differently across patient populations.

r001.rationale: It says health care makes harm more concrete by tying it to patient decisions and consequences, contrasting that with general checks such as offensiveness or factual errors.

r002.rationale: It discusses medical decisions and evaluating the surrounding system, but does not identify an assumption that models will not be used for medical decision-making or connect that assumption to blind spots in general-purpose evaluations.
